cross.title: The Birth and Early Feedback of Massive Star Clusters Across the Local Universe
cross.summary: Young massive star clusters (YMCs; ${\gtrsim}10^4\rm\,M_\odot$) represent a distinct, extreme mode of star formation and the closest present-day analogues of the environments in which globular clusters and Cosmic Noon stellar populations assembled. Given the extreme dust extinction in the earliest phase of YMC formation, (sub-)millimeter observations are the only means of probing their assembly and early feedback. Pioneering works with ALMA are limited to individual region studies and to the most massive YMCs in them, leaving many open questions about the initial conditions of YMC formation, the integrated star and cluster formation efficiencies, the dominant pre-supernova feedback channels, and the prevalence and reach of cluster-driven outflows. ALMA2040 will enable mass-complete, resolved surveys in hundreds of host galaxies, transforming the study of massive cluster formation and feedback from individual case analyses into statistical measurements across the full range of galactic environments.

The middle panel also shows P-Cygni profiles of the high-critical-density, optically thin CS (7–6) line, indicative of molecular outflows in three YMCs. The right panel overlays the location of ALMA-identified YMCs on the large-scale gas reservoir traced by CO (3–2). While current instrumental capabilities only allow individual region studies and access to the high-mass tail of YMC populations, ALMA2040 will entirely change the landscape by enabling mass-complete YMC censuses over hundreds of diverse host systems.

cross.title: Unveiling star formation at sub-solar metallicity with ALMA2040
cross.summary: A fundamental question in astrophysics is whether the processes governing star formation are universal or depend on the physical conditions of their local galactic environment. The Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds offer ideal laboratories to explore this question, as the gas conditions in them span up to orders of magnitude in metallicity, gas surface density, ambient pressure, dust abundance, radiation field, and cosmic-ray flux. In particular, both the outer Milky Way and the Magellanic clouds provide the closest low-metallicity environments with conditions similar to those of metal-poor galaxies, while remaining sufficiently close to soon allow spatial resolution of individual star-forming cores and disks. Recent observations with ALMA and other facilities have begun to unveil the physical and chemical properties of star-forming regions in low-metallicity environments. Yet, their distances from the Sun still require transformational gains in current ALMA capabilities to address fundamental open questions: (1) Are the properties of prestellar cores universal? (2) Does cloud fragmentation, and the resulting stellar IMF, depend critically on metallicity? (3) How does dust evolution depend on metallicity, and what is the impact in the survival of protoplanetary disks? (4) Is the reduced amount of metals and dust shielding at low metallicity critical for the formation and survival of molecules? ALMA2040 will identify similarities and differences between solar- and sub-solar-metallicity star-forming regions, and answer the question: how do different environmental conditions influence the physical and chemical pathways leading to star formation?

cross.title: Resolving the Assembly of Disk Galaxies from the Epoch of Reionisation to Cosmic Noon
cross.summary: Most of the mass and angular momentum of today's disk galaxies assembled at $z>1$. Yet, it remains unclear how these galaxies acquired their gas, how their baryons and dark matter coevolved, and how feedback and radial gas transport shaped their disks. Addressing these gaps requires resolved observations of cold gas, which carries most of the mass and angular momentum involved in galaxy assembly. By resolving CO and [C II] at kpc scales, ALMA revealed a surprising population of rotation-dominated disks, even at $z>2$, exhibiting kinematic signatures consistent with spiral arms, bars, and tidal tails. Yet, these studies are limited to massive ($M_\star>10^{10.5}$ M$_\odot$) and highly star-forming (SFRs$\gtrsim 100$ M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$) galaxies, the progenitors of today's most massive elliptical and disk galaxies. To understand how most present-day spirals (like the Milky Way) assembled, it is crucial to resolve their low-mass progenitors, which dominate the star-forming galaxy population by number at $z>1$. Achieving this goal demands a tenfold increase in line sensitivity and hence a next-generation sub-/millimetre facility: ALMA2040. This leap in sensitivity will enable routine resolved studies of hundreds of $M_\star>10^9$ M$_\odot$ galaxies, including those on and below the main sequence of star-forming galaxies, providing representative, statistical galaxy samples with sub-kpc constraints on the cold gas kinematics and morphology. By uniquely providing resolved CO, [C I], and [C II] observations across $z=1-6$, ALMA2040 will trace a much larger fraction of the cold-gas reservoir than is accessible today, extending resolved studies from rare massive and/or lensed systems to representative galaxy populations. In this way, ALMA2040 will transform our understanding of how galaxy disks formed and evolved.

cross.title: Dust at cosmic dawn: unveiling the onset of dust and obscured star formation at $z\gtrsim8$
cross.summary: Although less than 1 percent of the baryonic mass budget of a galaxy, cosmic dust profoundly alters the multi-wavelength appearance of galaxies across cosmic time. The (sub)millimeter wavelength regime is uniquely capable of weighing these dust reservoirs, and revealing the total extent of galaxy evolution that remains hidden behind them. With current facilities, however, doing so at $z > 8$ is largely out of reach. ALMA2040, a next-generation (sub)millimeter interferometer, is set to change this. Through an order-of-magnitude increase in sensitivity compared to ALMA, ALMA2040 is a transformational facility that will be able to routinely detect dust emission from galaxies at $z > 8$ and, through simultaneous multi-band characterization, accurately measure their dust masses, temperatures, and infrared luminosities. Combined with ancillary metallicity measurements -- including from the far-infrared lines detected by ALMA2040 itself -- this will establish the relative roles of supernovae and grain growth in building up dust in the earliest galaxies. Simultaneously, ALMA2040 will measure the fraction of star formation that is obscured by dust at cosmic dawn, and thereby the extent to which rest-UV and optical surveys miss early galaxy build-up. Without a 10$\times$ upgrade to ALMA -- comparable to the leap from the VLT to the ELT -- we will not be able to capitalize on the momentous advances enabled by JWST, and will remain blind to the cold and obscured component of galaxy formation in the $z > 8$ Universe.

cross.title: Probing cold gas and dust in quiescent galaxies across cosmic time
cross.summary: The discovery of massive quiescent galaxies at high redshift by JWST has revealed that star formation can cease rapidly in the early Universe, yet the physical mechanisms responsible for quenching remain unknown. A key missing element is the systematic measurement in statistically representative quiescent samples of the cold gas and dust content, which are crucial for distinguishing quenching mechanisms and evolutionary pathways. Such observations are currently not feasible because state-of-the-art sub-millimeter facilities (e.g., ALMA) cannot routinely detect the faint molecular gas and dust reservoirs of quiescent galaxies, nor pinpoint outflowing molecular gas. A next-generation facility (ALMA2040) capable of providing transformative access to the cold interstellar medium of quiescent galaxies across redshift is therefore essential. In particular, it will allow the community to probe the molecular gas content of quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon and beyond by targeting the CO, [CI], and [CII] emission lines, as well as unveiling the physical conditions of the cold interstellar medium by constraining the CO spectral line energy distribution. It will also reveal the dust content of the passive population, a crucial ingredient to constrain the different quenching mechanisms. Finally, it will enable probing the molecular gas kinematics and identify molecular outflows driven by supermassive black holes. When combined with the rich legacy of JWST, ELT, and SKAO surveys, ALMA2040 will deliver a comprehensive, multi-phase view of feedback and quenching, allowing us to establish when, how, and why galaxies shut down their star formation across cosmic time.

cross.title: Direct measures of black hole masses through cosmic time
cross.summary: Supermassive black holes (BHs) are thought to reside in all massive galaxies. They play a fundamental role in shaping galaxy evolution by suppressing star formation and halting the stellar growth of the most massive galaxies via feedback mechanisms. However, to date, measuring even their most basic property, their mass, is still challenging. The mass of BHs carries information on the growth history and the mutual interplay with the host galaxy. Uncertain BH masses leave many key questions on galaxy evolution wide open. Here we show that a transformational facility such as ALMA2040 would open a new window to measure BH mass by directly observing the kinematics of cold gas in galaxy cores from the local Universe up to very high redshift, irrespective of BH activity. This would revolutionise our understanding of BH formation, growth, and their role within galaxy evolution.

cross.title: Tracking the flow of interstellar gas across scales: from galaxies to star clusters
cross.summary: While the baryon cycle of the interstellar medium - and its ability to form stars - plays a key role in galaxy evolution, unravelling the physical processes driving its evolution remains a critical challenge, given that present-day observing facilities are unable to map entire galactic ecosystems down to the scales of individual star-forming clumps. Here, we outline the technical requirements that would enable, for the first time, to connect the small (pc) scale physics of star formation, to the large (tens-of-kpc) scales of galaxies, enabling an effective tracking of the flows of matter and energy across a vast range of environments, and answering the long-standing question of what regulates star formation across cosmic time.

cross.title: AGN Feeding and Feedback: Resolving the Torus
cross.summary: Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) play a key role in galaxy evolution by regulating star formation within their host galaxies. It is therefore crucial to understand how the central supermassive black holes (SMBH) are fueled by material from the galactic disk, and how AGN feedback impacts the surrounding gas. Most information so far comes from very nearby active galaxies (z < 0.008; D < 35 Mpc), providing the best spatial resolution and revealing randomly oriented dusty molecular tori that fuel SMBHs. A facility such as ALMA2040, offering significantly higher sensitivity and better angular resolution than current ALMA, would enable progress in two fundamental areas that remain beyond the capabilities of all existing and planned observatories: (i) probing the dynamics of the material feeding the AGN down to the accretion disk in nearby galaxies; and (ii) spatially resolving the tori and circum-nuclear regions of more energetic and cosmologically significant AGN, such as local quasars (z ~ 0.1 and Lbol > 10^45 erg/s).

cross.title: Molecular atlas of nearby galaxies through sensitive high-resolution multi-band molecular line surveys
cross.summary: Star formation and associated feedback processes play a key role in galaxy evolution. Astrochemistry is a powerful tool for characterising the physical conditions of dense star-forming gas and understanding the reciprocal relation between stellar feedback and the interstellar medium (ISM): from the way feedback influences the ISM to how the ISM conditions regulate the formation of new stars. The advent of large spectral surveys of a few individual galaxy centres have demonstrated the potential of molecular gas inventories to reveal the physical conditions of star-forming gas in great detail. A next-generation (sub)mm facility in the 2040s would extend this science to the local star-forming galaxy population, providing for the first time a comprehensive view of the physical and chemical conditions of the molecular ISM in the local universe.

figures.caption: : Key questions remain to be addressed to understand fully how the physical conditions of the dense SF-gas across and within galaxies. Molecular surveys at GMC scales are only available towards a few galactic centres and limited to a few range of frequencies. Studies about fractionation are scarce while they could bring crucial insights about the role of nucleosynthesis on galaxy’s chemistry and on SF history. The ALCHEMI survey ( Martín et al. 2021 ) showed the importance of targeting different molecular species to trace different SF-feedback-related processes at GMC scales. Such a study needs to be expanded to the local galaxy population, where we know GMCs’ physical properties vary (e.g. PHANGS-ALMA; Leroy et al. 2021 ), to get – for the first time – a comprehensive view of the ISM’s physical and chemical properties across the local universe.

cross.title: Minkowski Functionals of CII Line Intensity Maps: Probing Astrophysics and Primordial Features
cross.summary: Line intensity mapping aims to measure the total cumulative light of spectral lines from galaxies, without resolving individual sources. In this work, we investigate mock intensity maps of ionized carbon CII using Minkowski functionals, which capture the morphological properties of the maps. We generate semi-numerical simulations of CII intensity maps at $z\approx 6$ and $7.6$, adopting an astrophysical model that relates CII line luminosity to the mass of the host dark matter halos. We find that Minkowski functionals can provide tight constraints on the astrophysical model parameters in the presence of noise characteristics expected from the upcoming CCAT survey. We further investigate the prospects of probing a bump-like feature superimposed on the standard single power-law primordial power spectrum. Using a Fisher matrix formalism, we demonstrate that the effects of this primordial feature can be disentangled from those of the astrophysical model parameters. Combining measurements across multiple smoothing scales as well as redshifts can further improve the constraints and enhance the prospects for detecting such primordial features.

cross.title: From local chemistry to galactic evolution: unlocking the power of interstellar isotopes with ALMA2040
cross.summary: Molecular isotopic ratios provide a unique window into the chemical evolution of the interstellar medium, linking stellar nucleosynthesis and Galactic chemical evolution to the physical and chemical processes shaping molecular clouds, star-forming regions, and planetary systems. However, molecular isotopic ratios do not necessarily trace the underlying elemental composition, as chemical isotopic fractionation, isotope-selective photodissociation, grain chemistry, and radiative-transfer effects can significantly alter the observed values. Disentangling these effects requires simultaneous observations of multiple transitions, isotope systems and molecular families, including rare, doubly, and multiply substituted isotopologues involving D, $^{13}$C, $^{15}$N, $^{17,18}$O, $^{29,30}$Si, and $^{33,34,36}$S (e.g., $^{13}$C$^{15}$N, $^{13}$C$^{34}$S, and $^{13}$C$^{18}$O). ALMA2040, with an order-of-magnitude improvement in sensitivity and at least 512 GHz of instantaneous bandwidth, will make these species accessible across statistically significant samples of Galactic and nearby extragalactic sources. By enabling systematic isotopic inventories from molecular clouds and prestellar cores to protoplanetary systems, across the Milky Way and in external galaxies, ALMA2040 will establish molecular isotopes as quantitative probes of chemical inheritance, stellar nucleosynthesis, and galaxy evolution, disentangling local chemical processing from the large-scale evolution of matter from stars to new planetary systems.

cross.title: ALMA2040: The High-Redshift Circumgalactic Medium. Imaging the fueling and feedback of galaxies in the early universe
cross.summary: Galaxies do not form in isolation, but rather as part of a wider interconnected web mediated at their interface by an extended gaseous atmosphere - the Circum-Galactic Medium (CGM). This dynamic and multiphase region is fed and shaped by gas inflows and mergers from the intergalactic medium and by feedback-driven outflows and radiation from the central galaxy. The CGM is imprinted by the past, present and future evolution of its central galaxy and environment. The cool atomic and molecular phases are of particular interest as they dominate the mass budget of outflows and provide a reservoir of direct star forming fuel for the galaxy to accrete. In the early universe where accretion rates, mergers, and feedback processes peak, the cycle of gas through the CGM is most vigorous. Sub-mm observations have detected cold gas in extended halos and gas flows around high redshift galaxies but are thus far limited to the most massive, extreme or gravitationally lensed sources, using just a handful of the strongest emission and absorption lines. A significant increase ($5-10\times$) in spectral line sensitivity compared with the current ALMA is needed to push physical scales, densities and properties to a new regime. We present three key scientific cases for an ALMA2040 telescope: (i) direct imaging of extended [CII]-traced CGM halos around Milky-Way-progenitor galaxies at $z=4$-8; (ii) resolved detection of cold, clumpy outflows on $\sim$100 pc scales tied to individual star-forming clumps; and (iii) multi-species/-transition emission and absorption diagnostics that jointly constrain the density, chemistry, and radiation fields permeating the cool CGM and its multiphase gas flows.

cross.title: Frontiers of chemical complexity in the interstellar medium: unveiling the cosmic origins of life
cross.summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) contains a rich molecular inventory that provides a unique window into the chemistry operating during star and planet formation and its connection to prebiotic chemistry. More than 350 interstellar molecules are currently known, including increasingly complex organic molecules and species containing elements beyond the second row of the periodic table. Yet the limits that interstellar chemical complexity can reach, its evolution from molecular clouds to planetary systems, and its contribution to the molecular feedstock of life remain poorly constrained. Addressing these questions requires sensitive, broadband observations capable of detecting multiple weak rotational transitions of molecular species, such as amino acids, nucleobases, sugars and lipids, towards star- and planet-forming environments. Current facilities, including ALMA, are limited by instantaneous spectral coverage, sensitivity (especially on extended spatial scales), and the trade-off between total bandwidth and integration time. The proposed ALMA2040 facility would overcome these limitations through at least a tenfold improvement in spectral-line sensitivity, high-fidelity imaging from sub-arcsecond to tens-of-arcsecond scales, and ultra-broad instantaneous frequency coverage from 35 to 950 GHz at high spectral resolution. These capabilities would allow systematic detections of species with molecular abundances with respect to H$_2$ below 10$^{-11}$, facilitating the identification of new complex and heavy-element-bearing species through multiple transitions, and providing complete molecular inventories across evolutionary stages. ALMA2040 would thus make it possible to comprehensively investigate the emergence and evolution of chemical complexity, and to determine whether molecular precursors of prebiotic chemistry are widespread throughout the Galaxy.

cross.title: Star Formation across the Galaxy
cross.summary: Star formation is both a multi-scale and highly dynamic process. It is regulated by the combination of gravity, turbulence, feedback and magnetic fields, which connect more than six orders of magnitude in scale: from large molecular clouds (several 10s to 100s pc in size) down to protoplanetary disks (a few 10s to 100s of astronomical units in size, or 10^{-5} to 10^{-4} pc). Resolving the processes of fragmentation, accretion, and feedback that result in the formation of stellar systems throughout all relevant scales, from clouds to disks, and across the entire range of different environments in the Milky Way is key to constructing a comprehensive understanding and a predictive model of the formation process of stars of all masses that populate not only our Galaxy but the wider Universe across cosmic times. With current astronomical facilities, we are only able to grasp the details of star formation in <5% of Galactic star-forming regions, being heavily biased towards those close to us. Thus, characterizing this multi-scale phenomenon at the necessary sensitivity and resolution across all Galactic environments requires the next generation (sub)millimeter-wavelength facility: ALMA2040.

cross.title: Intermediate- and high-resolution optical spectroscopy on the nascent planetary nebula Vy 2-2: Evidence of binary-star evolution
cross.summary: Planetary nebulae (PNe) tend to show spectacular non-spherical shapes whose origin is not fully understood. Crucial information about PNe formation can be obtained by studying their very first stages. We present and analyze new intermediate- and échelle high-resolution spectra of the nascent PN Vy 2-2 to obtain its chemical abundances and a new value for its controversial Abundance Discrepancy Factor (ADF), investigate the internal kinematics and ionization of the nebula, and infer its possible formation processes. Our intermediate resolution spectra reveal many previously unreported nebular recombination (e.g., N$^+$) and forbidden (e.g., [F IV]) emission lines as well as stellar emission lines. Some of the newly detected nebular lines are important to determine the ADF. The derived abundances are subsolar and agree with previous values, while the new value of the ADF(O$^{2+}$)=13.6$\pm$2.6 indicates that Vy 2-2 belongs to the group of PNe with unusually high ADF. Our morphokinematical and ionization structure analysis reveals that Vy 2-2 consists of a relatively high-excitation central region and two low-excitation bipolar lobes. Our data does not show significant shock excitation in the main ionized shell of this PN. A distance of ~1.68 kpc to Vy 2-2 is obtained from the published angular expansion of the central region and its expansion velocity in H$^+$. The inferred kinematical age of ~210 yr supports that Vy 2-2 is a nascent PN. The stellar emission lines suggest a wels-like spectrum although more likely associated with an irradiated close companion than with the central star. Actually, the unusually high ADF, the observed nebular structures, presence of F, among others, point to Vy 2-2 hosting a post-common-envelope binary system. Chemical abundances and circumstellar mass estimates suggest an initial mass $\lesssim$0.9 $M_{\odot}$ for the star progenitor of Vy 2-2.

cross.title: Multi-wavelength Polarization as a Probe of Planet Formation
cross.summary: Polarization reveals details of circumstellar disks that are not readily available from total intensity observations. Via multi-wavelength polarimetric observations of disks, we can trace how planets form, how dust grains evolve at the onset of planet formation, and how magnetic fields (B-fields) influence accretion. Since polarized emission from these disks is typically at levels from 0.5% to a few percent of the total emission, very high sensitivities are needed. Current ALMA capabilities make these key measurements of protoplanetary disks challenging due to (1) long integrations with separate observations to measure multi-wavelength polarization of substructures, (2) prohibitive time requests to observe large samples of disks, (3) limited sensitivity and frequency coverage for polarization in spectral lines; and (4) insufficient calibration of polarization in all the Stokes parameters. An ALMA2040 with large collecting area, increased bandwidth with multi-band capabilities, and accurate polarization calibration will provide a great leap in our understanding of the formation of protoplanets through polarization. Specifically, such an ALMA2040 can use polarized emission from the continuum and spectral lines to: (A) provide stringent tests of streaming instabilities; (B) accurately constrain grain shape, size, porosity, and alignment; (C) resolve polarization of substructures for a large sample of disks with resolutions less than 5 au; (D) quickly survey 100s of disks; and (E) measure the B-field strength and morphology of disks.

cross.title: ALMA2040: Mapping the Spatially Resolved Dust and Star Formation Physics Driving High-z Galaxy Assembly
cross.summary: Interstellar dust reprocesses approximately half of the starlight emitted across cosmic history. However, dust temperature, which is essential to convert continuum flux into dust mass, molecular gas mass, and obscured star-formation rates, remains largely unconstrained on sub-galactic scales at high redshift. While single-band ALMA imaging has characterized continuum sizes for hundreds of z>1 galaxies, single-frequency measurements cannot separate the dust mass column from the local dust heating. To date, spatially resolved (<0.5-arcsec) multi-band dust temperatures exist in the literature for only ~10 extreme systems (quasars, hyperluminous starbursts, or strongly lensed galaxies) at z>1, with ongoing programs within a few years adding at most a few dozen submillimeter or UV-bright galaxies. This still leaves typical main-sequence disks largely unexplored across cosmic history. With an anticipated ~30 times improvement in continuum sensitivity (compared to the current ALMA), simultaneous multi-band receivers, and (sub-)kpc angular resolution, ALMA2040 will transform resolved dust thermometry into a systematic survey science. Here, we present the scientific rationale and technical requirements, highlighting a future statistically meaningful survey with > 100 representative main-sequence galaxies across cosmic epochs. Realistic visibility simulations demonstrate that ALMA2040 measures radial temperature gradients with ~0.5-4 K precision (L_IR~10^{12} L_sun in 2 h on-source at z~2). These measurements will break the degeneracy between intrinsic compactness and temperature gradients, deliver the first extinction-free, temperature-calibrated resolved star-formation relations, and uniquely trace radiative feedback and disk maturation from cosmic noon to cosmic dawn.

cross.title: High-frequency water megamasers as precision probes of black holes, galaxies and cosmology: A case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer
cross.summary: Water megamasers in the circumnuclear disks of active galactic nuclei are among the most precise probes of supermassive black holes. VLBI imaging of 22 GHz disk masers has provided geometric distances to independently constrain $H_0$, accurate black hole mass measurements, and sub-parsec views of accretion disk geometry. ALMA has opened a new window into water maser transitions in the sub-mm/mm regime, which trace temperatures, densities and disk regions that are inaccessible at 22 GHz, and can be observed at higher spatial resolution and with less free-free absorption. However, current detections are limited to a few bright extragalactic masers in nearby galaxies. We present the case for a next-generation sub-mm/mm interferometer - ALMA2040 - that would open a new parameter space for maser studies. We show that a 10-fold increase in line sensitivity and three times longer baselines compared to ALMA would transform sub-mm maser studies from a few bright detections into a population-level probe, delivering black hole masses and geometric distances from sub-mm masers alone, independent of and complementary to 22 GHz measurements. Integrated into a VLBI array, ALMA2040 would resolve maser disks out to $>$160 Mpc, extend maser black hole masses into the largely untested intermediate-mass regime, reveal magnetic field structure in accretion disks through polarization studies, and test systematics in $H_0$ measurements.

cross.title: A Sample of Thick-Disk Stars Hosting Hot Jupiters
cross.summary: We present a homogeneous analysis of 268 confirmed and candidate transiting hot-Jupiter host stars with 4800K < Teff < 6200K. We combine high-resolution TRES spectra, Gaia, 2MASS and WISE photometry, and Gaia astrometry to determine these stars' Teff, log g, Rstar, [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H]. Based on their [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H], we classify the stars as members of the Milky Way's low-[alpha/Fe] thin disk, high-[alpha/Fe] thick disk or an ambiguous intermediate population. We identify two confirmed hot Jupiters (WASP-81 b and TOI-5322 b) and three candidate hot Jupiters (TOI-3118.01, TOI-2728.01, and TOI-5781.01) as orbiting previously-unrecognized members of the high-alpha thick disk. We compare the properties of the confirmed planets in the three populations and note two indications of a potential difference between the populations: both high-[alpha/Fe] confirmed planets and eight out of the eleven ambiguous-disk confirmed planets are less massive than the median low-[alpha/Fe] planet, and none of our high-[alpha/Fe] or ambiguous confirmed planets have orbital periods shorter than 2.7 d, when 22% of our low-[alpha/Fe] population do. These differences may reflect variations in giant-planet formation across galactic environments, evolutionary effects, or differing stellar properties between the high- and low-[alpha/Fe] populations. Our catalog is the largest sample of chemically-identified high-[alpha/Fe] thick-disk confirmed and candidate hot-Jupiter host stars. These ancient systems, with ages > 8 Gyr, may allow for a better understanding of how the formation of hot Jupiters depends on galactic environment, and how their orbits evolve over very long time scales.

cross.title: Chemical Demographics of Star-forming Regions
cross.summary: Our understanding of complex organic chemistry during the formation of stars and planets is shaped by a handful of cherry-picked sources with bright molecular emission lines. This observational bias impedes our assessment of how universal chemical complexity is during star formation. The lack of systematic wideband spectral surveys for statistically significant samples of protostars and cores is a major roadblock to properly probing how COM inventories and abundances depend on the vast range of physical conditions, local cloud and global galactic environments, and evolutionary timescales of low- and high-mass star formation. In turn, this limits our ability to constrain and test physicochemical models, which depend critically on these parameters. The next-generation ALMA2040, with a 10x improvement in line sensitivity, is required to observe COMs, that we perceive as common today, in a fraction of the observing time that is needed today with ALMA. Such capabilities will propel us into the era of chemical demographics, whereby wideband (>100 GHz) spectral surveys at high sensitivity (routinely probing COM abundances down to 0.01% relative to CH3OH) will be executed towards >1000-10000 prestellar and protostellar sources. With robust chemical inventories towards large source sample sizes, we will be able to probe for dependencies of chemical complexity on mass regime, feedback processes in a cluster, Galactic position, metallicity, and time-variable accretion. Only with statistically significant samples at high sensitivity will we be able to assess the ubiquity and homogeneity of COM chemistry across the protostellar mass spectrum and natal cores. Constraining the diversity and availability of such species is critical for our understanding of the chemical reservoir available for planet formation, which eventually shapes (exo)planetary atmosphere compositions.

repl.title: Multi-phase investigation of outflows in the circumgalactic and interstellar media of luminous quasars at z~5
repl.summary: Aims. Outflows from active galactic nuclei are invoked as the principal feedback process regulating the co-evolution of supermassive black holes and their host galaxies. Because of their multi-phase and multi-scale nature, an exhaustive description of these winds should exploit multiple tracers. However, connecting various outflow features remains a challenge. The aim of this work is to provide a complete characterisation of outflows in a sample of z~5 quasars, by exploiting the combination of different emission and absorption tracers. Methods. We analysed the UV/optical and FIR continuum, line emission, and absorption in a sample of 39 z~5 quasars observed with VLT/X-Shooter and ALMA (available for six objects). We identified broad and narrow absorption lines associated with the quasar and emission lines to determine black hole masses and bolometric luminosities. Results. Our sample encompasses massive (log(M_BH,MgII / M_sun) = 8.5-10) and luminous (log(L_bol/(erg/s)) = 46.9-48) quasars at redshift 5.0-5.7. They display powerful ionised outflows detected in both emission and absorption, with velocities exceeding 48,000 km/s in some cases, and lie above the local black hole-host galaxy mass relation, exhibiting a behaviour similar to that of z~6 quasars. These findings suggest a phase of efficient black hole feedback occurring at redshift z~6 and likely persisting down to z~5, characterised by rapid black hole growth exceeding that of the host galaxy. The fraction of quasars with outflow detections in absorption is higher for larger CIV-MgII velocity shifts, suggesting that while the physical mechanisms powering the two outflow phenomena detected in emission and absorption may differ, a correlation exists between them.

repl.title: Barycenter kinematics in Local Group analogues
repl.summary: We investigate a new way to identify systems similar to our Local Group (LG) of galaxies in cosmological simulations. We use as an additional constraint the velocity of the LG barycenter, which is measured accurately from cosmic microwave background data. Using different cosmological simulations we compare pairs selected with this constraint to pairs selected with traditional methods. Our method selects simulated galaxy pairs where M31's radial approach speed to the Milky Way is 2% to 7% lower depending on the cosmology, while we find no robust change in the tangential velocity. The difference in the radial component is statistically significant in 86 of the 93 cosmological models we test, but the shift is small (a few kms$^{-1}$) compared to the typical velocity dispersion of LG analogues (tens of kms$^{-1}$). Matching the observed barycenter velocity therefore has a measurable but modest effect on LG analogue kinematics, and is best treated as an optional refinement, rather than a necessary selection criterion.

repl.title: Dark matter dynamical friction on binary stars in the faintest dwarf galaxies: I. Analytical approach
repl.summary: We study binary stars moving through a uniform dark matter background and experiencing dynamical friction. The centre-of-mass motion of the pairs is taken into account. We derive formulas and timescales for the secular evolution of the orbital parameters for both wide and close binaries. Applying these results to environments typical of the faintest ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, we show that some binaries undergo significant eccentricity oscillations while their semi-major axes gradually decrease over a Hubble time. At the population level, dynamical friction depletes wide binaries and increases the fraction of highly eccentric systems. Importantly, the effect is not strongest at the highest dark matter densities, since the associated increase in velocity dispersion weakens friction. With future, more detailed theoretical studies and improving observational capabilities, binary stars may serve as a tool to probe the dark matter content of the faintest galaxies.

repl.title: Dissecting the 3D chemo-dynamical structures of NGC~1381: A galaxy hosting an ancient slow bar with an accretion-related bulge and thick disc
repl.summary: We applied the barred population-orbit superposition method developed in our 2025 papers to construct 3D chemo-dynamical models for the barred S0 galaxy NGC~1381 in the Fornax cluster. Based on the stellar orbits in the models, we decomposed NGC~1381 into six components: (1) a dynamically warm nuclear disc with $f_{\rm nucl}\sim5\%$; (2) a rigidly rotating, BP/X-shaped bar with $f_{\rm bar}\sim30\%$; (3) a dynamically hot, spheroidal bulge with $f_{\rm bulge}\sim17\%$; (4) a dynamically cold thin disc with $f_{\rm thin}\sim28\%$; (5) a vertically extended thick disc with $f_{\rm thick}\sim16\%$; and (6) a dynamically hot, spatially diffuse stellar halo with $f_{\rm halo}\sim5\%$. The nuclear disc, bar, and thin disc are metal-rich ($[Z/\rm H]\gtrsim0$), $\alpha$-poor ($\rm[Mg/Fe]\lesssim0.2$), and old ($\sim13\rm\,Gyr$), corresponding to in situ formation in the early Universe. The bulge, thick disc, and stellar halo are metal-poor ($[Z/\rm H]\lesssim0$), $\alpha$-rich ($\rm[Mg/Fe]\gtrsim0.2$), and younger than or comparable in age to the in situ components, suggesting ex situ formation via minor mergers. Further analysis of stellar population gradients reveals that the thick disc and stellar halo, with their flat metallicity and [Mg/Fe] gradients, are likely dominated by a similar ex situ population. In contrast, the bulge exhibits a negative metallicity gradient ($\nabla[Z/\rm H]_{bulge}<0$), which might originate from either predominantly ex situ stars or a mixture of in situ and ex situ stars; its ex situ fraction cannot be quantified with the current data. Our modelling also reveals a slow bar ($\mathcal{R}=2.40_{-0.27}^{+0.54}$), with a bar pattern speed of $\rm\Omega_p=34_{-7}^{+4}\,km\,s^{-1}\,kpc^{-1}$, a bar length of $R_{\rm bar}=2.24_{-0.22}^{+0.43}\rm\,kpc$, and a corotation radius of $R_{\rm CR}=5.38_{-0.28}^{+1.59}\rm\,kpc$, consistent with its ancient formation time.

repl.title: A Deep Look at the Ultra-Faint Milky Way Satellite Virgo III with Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2
repl.summary: We analyze the ultra-faint Milky Way satellite Virgo III using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2 (DP2). Virgo III was observed in the Rubin "Cosmic Treasure Chest" (M49) First Look field, which contains 924 visits in the u,g,r,i bands comprising ~10.5hrs of exposure time with LSSTCam. These data are considerably deeper than the majority of DP2, with a $5\sigma$ limiting magnitude that approaches the expected 10-year depth of LSST (~25.2-26.5mag, depending on band). We report the morphological and stellar population parameters of Virgo III measured with the maximum-likelihood-based package ugali. The depth of the Rubin imaging yields more than a factor of four increase in the number of candidate member stars ($N_* = 114^{+11}_{-11}$) relative to the Virgo III discovery results ($N_* = 25^{+5}_{-4}$), enabling significantly more precise morphological constraints. Our best-fit parameters broadly agree with previous measurements, further confirming that Virgo III has properties that are consistent with an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy ($M_V = -2.72^{+0.49}_{-0.70}$; $r_{1/2} = 53^{+10}_{-8}$) located at a heliocentric distance of $D_\odot = 151^{+8}_{-8}$. We also demonstrate that the depth and photometric quality of the DP2 data are sufficient to separate metal-poor and metal-rich stars in color-color space. We further present period estimates for the three known RR Lyrae member stars derived from the DP2 forced photometry; we use theoretical Period-Luminosity-Metallicity (PLZ) and Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity (PWZ) relations to obtain independent distance estimates. We find that our period and distance estimates are broadly consistent with previous measurements for these RR Lyrae. These results demonstrate the power of LSST data for the discovery and characterization of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and motivate future searches for new satellites across the southern sky.

repl.title: ATLAS. III. Dust Around Little Red Dots: Hydrogen Line Ratios beyond Dust-free Non-Case B Models
repl.summary: We investigate broad hydrogen line ratios in little red dots (LRDs) using five high-redshift ($z>2$) sources from JWST/NIRSpec medium/high-resolution spectra in the DAWN JWST Archive and fifteen low-redshift sources ($z=0.1$--$0.9$) from the literature, all with broad H$\beta$ detected at $>5\sigma$. After carefully measuring the broad-line fluxes while accounting for absorption features and neighboring emission lines, we find that the broad H$\alpha$/H$\beta$ ratios are very high, ranging from 6 to 30, well above the Case B recombination value. Using plane-parallel \textsc{Cloudy} photoionization models with the total line emission from both sides of the slab, we investigate the physical origin of the broad hydrogen line ratios beyond Case B, jointly modeling the Balmer and Paschen line ratios for the subset of one high-$z$ and two low-$z$ LRDs with detected broad Paschen lines. We find that one low-$z$ LRD is reproduced by a high gas number density ($\log (n_{\mathrm H}/{\rm cm^{-3}})\sim10$--11) on the broad-line H$\alpha$/H$\beta$--Pa$\beta$/Pa$\gamma$ plane, whereas the remaining two LRDs additionally require substantial dust extinction of $E(B-V)\gtrsim0.2$, even after accounting for non-Case B effects. Since the narrow H$\alpha$/H$\beta$ ratios do not indicate such large dust extinction, these results demonstrate that the obscuring dust is spatially associated with the broad-line region. Even without Paschen-line measurements, two and eight LRDs in the high- and low-redshift samples, respectively, exhibit H$\alpha$/H$\beta>13$, which cannot be reproduced by the non-Case B models, suggesting that dust obscuration might be common among LRDs, occurring in at least about half of the population. Such dust may represent a lower-column-density counterpart of the dusty torus in AGNs, reconciling the weak hot-dust emission.

repl.title: Confidently Wrong: Why Ignoring Binaries Biases IMF Inference at Large Sample Sizes
repl.summary: The stellar initial mass function (IMF) high-mass slope $\alpha$ is routinely measured by fitting single-star models to photometric samples that contain unresolved binaries. This practice introduces a systematic negative bias on $\alpha$ that is constant with sample size $N$. Posterior credible intervals shrink as $1/\sqrt{N}$, so at sufficiently large $N$ the bias exceeds the full 95% credible-interval width and the true value falls outside the credible interval - a regime we call "confidently wrong." Building on earlier studies of the bias magnitude, we quantify the sample size at which this bias exceeds the statistical uncertainty. We quantify this bias using two idealized observation operators: mass-addition ($m_{\mathrm{obs}}=m_1+m_2$), a formal upper bound on unresolved-system mass overestimation, and luminosity-addition ($m_{\mathrm{obs}}=L^{-1}(L_1+L_2)$), an idealized lower-bias photometric case based on the ZAMS mass-luminosity relation. Across four astrophysical environments spanning $\alpha=1.60$-$2.30$, we find: (1) mass-addition bias of 0.054-0.086 with crossover to confidently wrong at $N_{\mathrm{cross}}\sim5{,}000$-$10{,}000$; (2) luminosity-addition bias of 0.011-0.021 with $N_{\mathrm{cross}}\sim75{,}000$-$150{,}000$; and (3) a binary-aware mixture likelihood that marginalizes over the Moe & Di Stefano (2017) binary population model recovers the true slope in the synthetic tests presented here. Published single-star IMF slopes can therefore plausibly carry systematic errors of order 0.01-0.09 if unresolved binaries are not modeled, comparable to or exceeding reported uncertainties in some regimes. Since current and upcoming surveys (Gaia, JWST, Roman, LSST) will deliver large resolved-star samples, binary-aware inference is likely necessary to avoid binary-driven systematic bias in the large-$N$ single-star-fitting regime.

repl.title: Mock Catalogs of Strongly Lensed Gravitational Waves via a Halo Model Approach with Space-borne Detectors
repl.summary: Future space-borne gravitational-wave (GW) detectors, such as LISA and DECIGO, are expected to detect a large number of GW events, a fraction of which may be strongly lensed by intervening galaxies or galaxy clusters. In this work, we develop a comprehensive framework to simulate strongly lensed GWs in the context of space-borne detectors. Based on realistic astrophysical models for both the source population and the lens distribution, we construct mock catalogs of lensed GW events, referred to as \textbf{GW-LMC-Space}. Our results show that, for a four-year LISA observation, the expected number of lensed events ranges from $0$ to $131$, depending on the adopted formation model of massive black hole binaries (MBHBs). The corresponding lensing probability for MBHBs can reach up to $\sim 0.3\%$. For DECIGO, we find that the number of lensed events in a one-year observation is expected to lie in the range of $0$--$44$, with a lensing probability of $\sim 0.15\%$ for stellar-mass binary black holes (BBHs), binary neutron stars (BNSs), and neutron star--black hole binaries (NSBHs). We further show that the overlap of lensed signals is a common feature in space-borne detectors, which can significantly affect both the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) estimation and event identification. These results highlight the importance of accounting for signal overlap in the analysis of strongly lensed GW events in future space-borne GW observations.

repl.title: A binary black hole merger rate comparison within the same metallicity-star formation rate framework
repl.summary: Recent studies have suggested that binary population synthesis models, when coupled with observationally based, metallicity-dependent SFRD, overpredict the observed local BBH merger rate density. The significance of this tension might vary depending on the specific code and parameters adopted. Thus, a more extensive exploration of the parameter space is required. Here, we perform such an extended analysis. We first carry out a comprehensive analysis by using a large set of BBH merger efficiencies across a wide range of physical assumptions, parameters, and initial conditions. We combine these efficiencies with an observationally motivated SFRD and explore 18 metallicity variations to encompass observational uncertainties. We find that the tension between predicted and observed BBH merger rate density persists: in 17 out of 18 metallicity variations none of the models considered predicts a local BBH merger rate within or below the observed 90% credible interval. Even in the most favorable metallicity variation, only <10% of the models are consistent with the observational constraints. Then, we perform a full calculation, including a self-consistent delay time distribution, for the models yielding the lowest BBH merger rate densities. This analysis confirms that even the most conservative models overpredict the observed local BBH merger rate for almost all the metallicity variations. We show that the inclusion of the low-metallicity tail contributed by low-mass galaxies and starbursts, together with a treatment of iron rather than oxygen abundance, systematically shift the predicted rates toward higher values. Consequently, even literature models that predict moderate BBH merger rates can instead produce substantially higher rates when coupled to an observationally motivated SFRD.

repl.title: The Kick Velocities of Neutron Stars in Binary Systems
repl.summary: Neutron stars (NSs) receive natal kicks on their formation in supernovae (SNe). We consider constraints placed on the natal kick magnitudes by NSs in different classes of binary systems. We compare observed systems to predictions from the COMPAS rapid population synthesis code, where we apply kick models with varied natal kick prescriptions. Specifically, we compare binary orbits (i.e., periods and eccentricities) and systemic kick estimates of (1) Gaia observations of NS-harboring binaries (Gaia NSs), (2) NS low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs), (3) NS-white dwarf binaries (NSWDs), (4) NS high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) and in particular Be X-ray binaries (BeXBs), and (5) double NSs (DNSs). In this comparison, we find that we can reproduce most of the observed properties of the Gaia NSs, LMXBs, and NSWDs with natal kicks calibrated to the velocities of young isolated pulsars, although we need a small amount of "rocket" kicks to explain the Gaia NS eccentricities. The HMXBs and DNSs, in contrast, show evidence of significantly reduced NS natal kicks. In particular, we find that an apparent correlation between eccentricity and systemic kick for DNSs can be explained by Blaauw kicks, if the natal kicks are $\lesssim 10$ km s$^{-1}$. Although our model does not align well with low-metallicity Gaia NSs, high-eccentricity BeXBs, and DNS mass estimates, we provide alternative hypothetical explanations for these systems. We conclude that a model in which NSs that are formed in binaries with high-mass companions receive significantly reduced natal kicks can provide a relatively consistent explanation for the observed NSs in binary systems.

repl.title: JWST lensed quasar dark matter survey V: Hints of self-interacting dark matter from 29 quadruply imaged quasars
repl.summary: Theories of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) predict the eventual core collapse of dark matter halos, a process that transforms these structures into extremely efficient gravitational lenses. We present a population-level inference on the abundance of core collapsed halos and subhalos in the mass range $10^6 - 10^{10.7} M_{\odot}$ using 29 quadruply imaged quasars, drawing on the collective lensing signal of many low-mass perturbers. Our structure formation model predicts the abundance of collapsed (sub)halos as a function of halo mass and redshift. We quantify how our results are affected by systematic uncertainties, including the abundance of globular clusters (GCs) and subhalos, and the internal structure of deeply collapsed halos. Our data exhibits a strong preference for core collapsed halos in the lens model, with Bayes factors disfavoring CDM relative to SIDM ranging from 8:1 to 24:1, depending on the assumed SIDM subhalo abundance and the internal structure of collapsed halos. Explaining our data without core collapse requires both a GC abundance well above expectations and more subhalos than predicted by $N$-body simulations. These results pose a challenge to the CDM paradigm. We present a particle physics interpretation of these results in a companion paper.

The center panel has median collapse timescales t 6 / 8 = 50 ​ Gyr t_{6/8}=50\ \rm{Gyr} and t 8 / 10 = 2 ​ Gyr t_{8/10}=2\ \rm{Gyr} , driving core collapse primarily in halos more massive than 10 8 ​ M ⊙ 10^{8}M_{\odot} . The panel on the right has t 6 / 8 = 2 ​ Gyr t_{6/8}=2\ \rm{Gyr} and t 8 / 10 = 50 ​ Gyr t_{8/10}=50\ \rm{Gyr} , causing the collapse of low-mass halos. figures.caption: Lens models that reproduce the flux ratios of J0924, a system with a strong flux anomaly (demagnification) in image D. We highlight these three particular examples out of millions of lens models generated for this system in our analysis to illustrate different possible explanations for the data. Our forward modeling approach quantifies the relative likelihood of these possible solutions. Top panels: The substructure convergence map of the lens system. Dark matter and globular cluster parameters are listed in the top left inset, macromodel parameters in the top center inset, and the strengths of m = 1 m=1 , m = 3 m=3 , and m = 4 m=4 multipole perturbations to the main deflector mass profile are shown in the top right. Image positions are labeled A-D, with model-predicted (black) and measured (green) flux ratios listed alongside each image. Lower panels: The four panels below each convergence map show zoomed-in regions of the convergence map around images A and D, and the lensed quasar images computed by ray tracing through the lens systems. Globular clusters, subhalos, and line-of-sight halos produce the various small-scale features visible in the convergence maps. Line-of-sight halos appear sheared and distorted in the convergence maps due to coupling between their deflection angles and the main deflector. In the lower panels, we highlight the perturber that most strongly affects the magnification of image D.
